idolatrous

/eye-DOL-uh-truss/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Idolatrous means worshipping someone or something excessively, as if it were a god — a word with a built-in warning.

The franchise's most idolatrous fans refused to admit the new film had a single flaw.

Worked Example

When chef Duval opened his third restaurant, his line cooks stopped tasting the food before it left the kitchen. "If he wrote the recipe, it's perfect," one shrugged, and any server who suggested a dish was over-salted got frozen out of the group chat. A visiting food writer observed that the kitchen's devotion had become idolatrous: the staff no longer served customers — they served a man they had quietly turned into a god.

The cooks' refusal to taste or question anything — treating Duval's word as perfect by definition — is what pushes their devotion past loyalty into idolatrous worship.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

worshipful: Worshipful means showing reverent, awed adoration, as if before something divine -- but the word itself passes no judgment: a worshipful hush in a cathedral can be perfectly fitting. Idolatrous is worshipful devotion plus a verdict -- the word itself declares that the admiration has gone inappropriately far and turned a person into a god.

fanatical: Fanatical means devoted beyond all reason, and it measures pure intensity -- a fanatical jogger or fan is simply extreme about the thing. Idolatrous says something more specific: the devotion has become worship, treating a person or thing as a god. Fanatical describes how hard the devotion runs; idolatrous accuses it of the wrong shape.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

skeptical: inclined to question and doubt

clear-eyed: seeing someone's real flaws honestly

Where it sits · how blind the devotion has become — admiring → idolatrous → cultish

admiring vs. idolatrous: Admiring is healthy appreciation that still sees flaws; idolatrous devotion has crossed the line into treating a person like a god.

cultish vs. idolatrous: Cultish goes even further than idolatrous, suggesting an entire closed group organized around blind worship.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — idol

Root — idol: an image worshipped as a god (Greek eidolon)

Root — latr

Root — latr: worship, service (Greek latreia)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of; characterized by

Put it together

Put it together: Idolatrous stacks two Greek roots: eidolon, 'an image worshipped as a god' (which also gives us idol and idolize), and latreia, 'worship or service.' Add the adjective suffix -ous and you get 'full of idol-worship' — which is why the word always carries a criticism: the admiration it describes has been aimed at something that doesn't deserve god-like treatment.

Use the root in a new word: idolize

Use the root in a new word: idolize: Fans who idolize an athlete treat him like something more than human — the same Greek root eidolon, 'an image worshipped as a god,' that builds idolatrous.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal, critical — carries a built-in warning

Idolatrous is never neutral praise: it signals that admiration has gone inappropriately far, unlike revere and venerable, which describe deep respect that stays healthy and deserved. Keep it in its own lane among this unit's praise words too — renown is earned fame, adulation is over-the-top gushing, and a commendation is an official act of praise, but idolatrous alone accuses the admirer of treating a person like a god.
